lessons.title: What is HTML and Web Pages
lessons.content:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the language used to create web pages. Every website you visit is built with HTML. HTML uses tags to structure content — tags are keywords in angle brackets like

for paragraph,

for heading. Most tags come in pairs:

This is text

. Every HTML page has a basic structure: , , (metadata, title), and (visible content). The browser reads the HTML and displays it as a web page. HTML is not a programming language — it's a markup language that structures content.
examples:
Welcome to My Website

— creates a large heading

This is a paragraph of text.

— creates a paragraph
— displays an image (self-closing tag)

keyTerms.tag: An HTML keyword in angle brackets that defines an element
keyTerms.element:
An HTML tag plus its content:

text

is a paragraph element
keyTerms.attribute: Extra information added to a tag: src, alt, href, class, id

quiz.question: What does HTML stand for?
quiz.explanation: HTML = HyperText Markup Language — the standard language for web pages.

quiz.question: Which tag creates the largest heading?
quiz.explanation: h1 is the largest heading, h6 is the smallest.

quiz.question: Where does visible content go in HTML?
quiz.explanation: The <body> tag contains everything the user sees on the page.

lessons.title: Text, Links, and Images
lessons.content:
HTML provides tags for all content types. Headings:

to

(largest to smallest). Paragraphs:

. Bold: or . Italic: or . Line break:
. Links use the anchor tag: Click here — the href attribute specifies the destination. Images: — src is the file path, alt is the text shown if the image can't load (also used by screen readers). Lists:

    for unordered (bullets),
      for ordered (numbers), with
    1. for each item.
examples: Go to page 2 — a link to another page

• Apples
  • Bananas
— a bullet list
Important: Always add alt text to images for accessibility

keyTerms.anchor tag: The <a> tag used to create hyperlinks with href attribute
keyTerms.href: The attribute specifying where a link goes
keyTerms.alt text: Alternative text for images — describes the image for accessibility

quiz.question: Which tag creates a hyperlink?
quiz.explanation: The <a> (anchor) tag with href attribute creates clickable links.

quiz.question: What does the alt attribute do on an image?
options: Provides text description if image can't load
quiz.explanation: Alt text describes the image for screen readers and when images fail to load.

quiz.question: <ol> creates what type of list?
quiz.explanation: ol = ordered list (1, 2, 3...), ul = unordered list (bullets).

lessons.title: Forms and Input
lessons.content: HTML forms collect user input. The <form> tag wraps all form elements. Common input types: <input type='text'> for text, type='password' for hidden text, type='email' for email validation, type='number' for numbers, type='checkbox' for toggles, type='radio' for single-choice options. <textarea> creates a multi-line text box. <select> creates a dropdown menu with <option> items. <button type='submit'> submits the form. The <label> tag describes each input for accessibility. Forms send data to a server when submitted.
examples: <input type='text' placeholder='Enter your name'> — text field with hint
<select><option>English</option><option>French</option></select> — dropdown
<input type='checkbox' id='agree'> <label for='agree'>I agree</label> — checkbox with label

keyTerms.form: An HTML element that collects and sends user input
keyTerms.input: A form element for various types of user data entry
keyTerms.placeholder: Hint text shown inside an input field before the user types

quiz.question: Which input type hides what the user types?
quiz.explanation: type='password' shows dots/asterisks instead of the actual characters.

quiz.question: What does <label> do?
quiz.explanation: Labels describe inputs — clicking a label focuses its associated input.

quiz.question: Which tag creates a dropdown menu?
quiz.explanation: <select> with <option> children creates a dropdown menu.

lessons.title: Introduction to CSS
lessons.content: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks — colors, fonts, spacing, layout. CSS rules have a selector and declarations: h1 { color: blue; font-size: 24px; }. Three ways to add CSS: inline (style attribute on an element), internal (<style> tag in <head>), or external (separate .css file linked with <link>). External is best — one file styles the entire website. Colors can be named (red), hex (#FF0000), or RGB (rgb(255,0,0)). The cascade means later styles override earlier ones, and more specific selectors win.
examples: p { color: #333; font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.6; } — styles all paragraphs
body { background-color: #f0f0f0; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; }
<link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'> — links an external CSS file

keyTerms.selector: The part of a CSS rule that targets HTML elements to style
keyTerms.property: What aspect to change (color, font-size, margin, padding)
keyTerms.cascade: The system that determines which styles win when rules conflict

quiz.question: What does CSS stand for?
quiz.explanation: CSS = Cascading Style Sheets — it styles HTML content.

quiz.question: Which is the best way to add CSS?
quiz.explanation: External CSS files keep styling separate and can be reused across pages.

quiz.question: What color is #FF0000?
quiz.explanation: FF in the red channel, 00 in green and blue = pure red.

lessons.title: Box Model and Layout
lessons.content: Every HTML element is a rectangular box with four layers: content (the actual text/image), padding (space between content and border), border (the edge of the box), and margin (space outside the border). Control size with width and height. Display property controls layout: block elements (div, p, h1) take full width; inline elements (span, a, strong) only take needed width. Flexbox (display: flex) makes layout easy — arrange items in rows or columns, center them, and distribute space. Grid (display: grid) creates two-dimensional layouts with rows and columns.
examples: div { padding: 20px; margin: 10px; border: 1px solid black; } — box model
.container { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; } — centers children
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 10px; } — 3 equal columns

keyTerms.box model: Content + padding + border + margin = the full space an element takes
keyTerms.flexbox: A CSS layout mode for arranging items in rows or columns flexibly
keyTerms.margin: Space outside an element's border, creating distance from other elements

quiz.question: In the box model, what is between content and border?
quiz.explanation: Padding is the space between the content and the border.

quiz.question: display: flex makes an element a:
quiz.explanation: display: flex turns an element into a flex container, enabling flexible child layout.

quiz.question: What does margin: auto do on a block element with set width?
quiz.explanation: Auto margins distribute remaining space equally, centering the element.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.content: Responsive design makes websites work on all screen sizes — phones, tablets, and desktops. Use the viewport meta tag: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>. Media queries apply different CSS at different screen widths: @media (max-width: 768px) { ... } targets screens 768px or narrower. Use relative units: % and vw/vh instead of fixed px. Flexbox and Grid naturally adapt. Mobile-first design means writing mobile styles first, then adding complexity for larger screens. Test on real devices or browser developer tools.
examples: @media (max-width: 600px) { .sidebar { display: none; } } — hides sidebar on mobile
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } — images scale to fit their container
.container { width: 90%; max-width: 1200px; margin: auto; } — responsive centered container

keyTerms.responsive design: Building websites that adapt to different screen sizes
keyTerms.media query: CSS rule that applies styles only at certain screen widths
keyTerms.viewport: The visible area of a web page on a device screen

quiz.question: What does @media (max-width: 768px) target?
quiz.explanation: max-width: 768px means the styles apply when the screen is 768px or narrower.

quiz.question: Why use % instead of px for widths?
quiz.explanation: Percentage widths adapt to the parent container size, making layouts responsive.

quiz.question: Mobile-first design means:
options: Write mobile styles first, then add desktop styles
quiz.explanation: Start with mobile layout, then use media queries to enhance for larger screens.

lessons.title: Variables and Functions in JS
lessons.content: JavaScript makes web pages interactive. Declare variables with let (changeable) or const (fixed): let score = 0; const name = 'Otic';. Data types: strings ('hello'), numbers (42), booleans (true/false), arrays ([1,2,3]), objects ({name: 'Alice', age: 15}). Functions: function greet(name) { return 'Hello ' + name; } or arrow syntax: const greet = (name) => 'Hello ' + name;. JavaScript runs in the browser — add it with <script> tags or link an external .js file. Console.log() prints output for debugging.
examples: let count = 0; count++; // count is now 1
const add = (a, b) => a + b; console.log(add(3, 5)); // 8
const fruits = ['apple', 'banana']; fruits.push('cherry'); // adds to array

keyTerms.let: Declares a variable whose value can be reassigned
keyTerms.const: Declares a variable whose value cannot be reassigned

quiz.question: What is the difference between let and const?
options: let can be reassigned, const cannot
const can be reassigned, let cannot
let is for numbers, const for strings
quiz.explanation: let allows reassignment; const creates a constant that can't be changed.

quiz.question: How do you add an item to an array in JS?
quiz.explanation: array.push(item) adds an item to the end in JavaScript.

quiz.question: Where does JavaScript run?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript runs in the browser to make web pages interactive (also on servers with Node.js).

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation
lessons.content: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's representation of your HTML as objects that JavaScript can read and change. Select elements: document.getElementById('myId'), document.querySelector('.myClass'), document.querySelectorAll('p'). Change content: element.textContent = 'New text'; or element.innerHTML = 'Bold';. Change styles: element.style.color = 'red';. Add/remove classes: element.classList.add('active');. Create elements: document.createElement('p'); and add them: parent.appendChild(newElement);. The DOM lets you update the page without reloading.
examples: document.getElementById('title').textContent = 'Welcome!'; — changes heading text
document.querySelector('.btn').style.backgroundColor = '#4F46E5'; — changes button color
const li = document.createElement('li'); li.textContent = 'New item'; list.appendChild(li); — adds list item

keyTerms.DOM: Document Object Model — the browser's tree representation of HTML elements
keyTerms.querySelector: A method to select the first element matching a CSS selector
keyTerms.innerHTML: Property to get or set the HTML content inside an element

quiz.question: What does DOM stand for?
quiz.explanation: DOM = Document Object Model — the browser's tree of HTML elements.

quiz.question: How do you select an element with id='header'?
quiz.explanation: getElementById selects a single element by its unique id attribute.

quiz.question: element.textContent = 'Hello' does what?
options: Changes the text inside the element
quiz.explanation: textContent sets the text content of an element, replacing whatever was there.

lessons.title: Events and Interactivity
lessons.content: Events are things that happen on a web page — clicks, key presses, form submissions, page loads. JavaScript listens for events and responds. Add event listeners: button.addEventListener('click', function() { alert('Clicked!'); });. Common events: click, mouseover, mouseout, keydown, keyup, submit, load, scroll. Event handlers can change the page, validate forms, show/hide elements, and more. The event object contains information about what happened: event.target (the element clicked), event.key (the key pressed). Prevent default behavior with event.preventDefault() — useful for form submission.
examples: btn.addEventListener('click', () => { count++; display.textContent = count; }); — click counter
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); // handle form data }); — prevent page reload
input.addEventListener('keyup', () => { results.textContent = input.value.toUpperCase(); }); — live transform

keyTerms.event listener: Code that waits for a specific event and runs a function when it occurs
keyTerms.event: An action or occurrence on a page: click, keypress, submit, load
keyTerms.preventDefault: Stops the browser's default behavior for an event

quiz.question: What method attaches an event handler to an element?
quiz.explanation: addEventListener('event', callback) is the standard way to listen for events.

quiz.question: event.preventDefault() is commonly used with:
options: Form submissions to prevent page reload
quiz.explanation: Forms normally reload the page on submit — preventDefault stops this.

quiz.question: Which event fires when a user presses a key?
quiz.explanation: keydown fires when a key is pressed; keyup fires when released.

lessons.title: Project Structure
lessons.content: A well-organized website has a clear folder structure. The root folder contains index.html (the homepage), a css/ folder for stylesheets, a js/ folder for JavaScript files, and an images/ folder for media. Use relative paths to link files: <link rel='stylesheet' href='css/style.css'>. Naming conventions: lowercase, hyphens instead of spaces (my-page.html). Every page needs: DOCTYPE declaration, html lang attribute, meta charset, viewport meta tag, a descriptive title, and linked CSS/JS files. Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer> instead of generic <div> everywhere.
examples:
project/
  index.html
  css/style.css
  js/app.js
  images/logo.png
<header><nav>Menu</nav></header><main><article>Content</article></main><footer>© 2024</footer>
<meta charset='UTF-8'>\n<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>

keyTerms.semantic HTML: Using meaningful tags (header, nav, main, footer) instead of generic divs
keyTerms.relative path: A file path relative to the current file location (css/style.css)
keyTerms.index.html: The default homepage file that servers look for in a directory

quiz.question: What is the standard filename for a website's homepage?
quiz.explanation: index.html is the convention — servers automatically serve it as the default page.

quiz.question: Which is a semantic HTML tag?
quiz.explanation: nav, header, main, footer are semantic — they describe their content's purpose.

quiz.question: Where should CSS files typically be placed?
quiz.explanation: A css/ folder keeps stylesheets organized and separate from HTML.

lessons.title: Version Control with Git
lessons.content: Git tracks changes to your code over time. Initialize: git init. Stage changes: git add filename. Commit (save snapshot): git commit -m 'Added navigation bar'. View history: git log. GitHub is an online platform to store and share Git repositories. Push to GitHub: git push. Pull changes: git pull. Branches let you work on features without affecting the main code: git branch feature-name, git checkout feature-name. When the feature is ready, merge it back. Git is essential for teamwork — multiple people can work on the same project without conflicts.
examples: git init — creates a new Git repository in the current folder
git add . && git commit -m 'Initial commit' — stages all files and commits
git checkout -b new-feature — creates and switches to a new branch

keyTerms.repository: A folder tracked by Git, containing all files and their change history
keyTerms.commit: A saved snapshot of your project at a point in time
keyTerms.branch: A parallel version of the code for developing features independently

quiz.question: What does 'git commit' do?
options: Saves a snapshot of staged changes
quiz.explanation: A commit saves the current state of staged files as a snapshot in history.

quiz.question: What is GitHub?
options: An online platform to host Git repositories
quiz.explanation: GitHub stores Git repositories online for sharing, collaboration, and backup.

quiz.question: Why use branches?
options: To work on features without affecting the main code
quiz.explanation: Branches isolate new work — merge back when it's ready and tested.

lessons.title: Deploying Your Website
lessons.content: Deployment means putting your website on the internet for everyone to see. Static sites (HTML/CSS/JS only) can be hosted for free on GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel. Steps for GitHub Pages: push code to GitHub, go to Settings → Pages, select the branch. Your site is live at username.github.io/repo-name. For custom domains, buy a domain name and point it to your host. Test before deploying: check all links work, images load, responsive design works on mobile. Use browser developer tools (F12) to test and debug. Performance matters: optimize images, minimize CSS/JS, use caching.
examples: GitHub Pages: push to main branch → Settings → Pages → site is live in minutes
Netlify: drag and drop your project folder → site deployed with free HTTPS
Custom domain: buy example.com → set DNS to point to your host → site available at example.com

keyTerms.deployment: Publishing a website to a server so it's accessible on the internet
keyTerms.hosting: A service that stores your website files and serves them to visitors
keyTerms.domain: The web address people type to visit your site (e.g., example.com)

quiz.question: Which service offers free static website hosting?
quiz.explanation: GitHub Pages hosts static sites (HTML/CSS/JS) for free directly from a repository.

quiz.question: What is deployment?
options: Publishing a website to the internet
quiz.explanation: Deployment is the process of putting your finished website online for public access.

quiz.question: What should you check before deploying?
options: Links, images, responsive design all work
quiz.explanation: Test everything: links, images, mobile view, forms, and performance before going live.
